item.title: Privileged helper
item.description:
Each app has a privileged helper: a root LaunchDaemon on macOS, a systemd service on Linux, the ClaimwardHelper service (LocalSystem) on Windows. It is the only privileged process of the app. All three are the same code, pkg/helper of claimward-vpn-client; each app supplies only a main that loads the configuration and listens.

The helper does the server communication as well as the tunnel: it enrolls, brings the tunnel up, and watches route pushes. On macOS “Local Network” privacy blocks an unprivileged app from a server on the LAN and root is exempt; the other platforms follow the same path so that the three apps behave alike.

The socket protocol

One JSON request per connection, one JSON response (pkg/hproto):

Action What the helper does
connect enrolls with the server named in the request, if its configuration allows it, with the bearer, private key, device name and tenant given; brings the tunnel up; watches the RouteService
tenants asks the server which tenants the bearer may connect to
down takes the tunnel down
status for each tunnel: the interface, the address, the tenant and, since v0.12.0, its live facts (see below)
approve since v0.11.0: approves the server named in the request, if the operating system consents (see Server approval)
revoke removes a server from the approved ones
approved lists the approved servers

Since v0.11.0 the helper holds one tunnel per server, each on its own interface, named from the server’s URL: on Windows the adapter is no longer called Claimward but Claimward <host> <6 hex> (a breaking change for anything that looked the adapter up by its old name).

What status reports per tunnel

Since v0.12.0 each tunnel in the answer carries, read-only, what a detail panel shows (the fields are omitted when empty):

Field Meaning
interface, assigned_ip the interface name and the address, apart from each other
endpoint the peer’s host:port, as the device holds it now
allowed_ips the CIDRs routed into the tunnel (they follow a route push)
dns, mtu the DNS servers the server assigned, and the interface’s MTU
rx_bytes, tx_bytes bytes the device received from and sent to the peer since the tunnel came up
last_handshake the last completed handshake (absent until there has been one)

The live values are read from the WireGuard device itself (the cross-platform UAPI get operation), so a roaming endpoint or a new route shows at once; if the device cannot be read, the enrollment’s values are reported and the counters stay at zero. The answer never contains a key or a bearer. As before, status lists every tunnel of the machine to any process allowed to use the socket: there is one set of tunnels, not one per user, so the new fields widen nothing. The apps poll it, once a second while a detail panel is open.

Bounded by its own configuration

Any process that can reach the helper’s socket can make it act, so what it does is bounded by its own configuration, never by the request:

  • It enrolls only with a server its configuration names, or one that was approved with the system’s consent. A helper that took the server from the request would let any local process point it at a server of its own, answering with routes for 0.0.0.0/0: every packet of the machine, sent where that process chose. Approval is the operating system’s own prompt (macOS Authorization Services, polkit on Linux, an elevated second socket on Windows), never a field of the request: see Server approval.
  • It takes no tunnel configuration from a request. The tunnel is what that server answered at enrollment. The earlier up and update-routes actions, which took one, are gone.
  • Its configuration must be root’s (SYSTEM’s or the Administrators’ on Windows) and writable by nobody else, or the helper does not start: whoever writes it chooses the servers trusted.
{
 "servers": ["https://vpn.example.org"],
 "group": "claimward",
 "socket": "/var/run/claimward-helper.sock"
}
Key
servers optional since v0.11.0: the servers pre-approved by the administrator (compared without a trailing /); others need approval
approvals optional: where the approved servers are kept (the default per platform is in Server approval)
group who may use the socket beside root: admin on macOS, claimward on Linux, Claimward Users on Windows by default
socket /var/run/claimward-helper.sock by default, C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.sock on Windows
Platform helper.json
macOS /Library/Application Support/Claimward/helper.json
Linux /etc/claimward/helper.json
Windows C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.json

The socket: macOS and Linux

The socket is 0660, owned by root and the helper’s group. It is created with a restrictive umask, so it never exists with a wider mode, in a directory only root can write (the helper refuses one somebody else could, since they could replace the socket with their own and receive the app’s bearer). The earlier helper’s socket was 0666.

The socket: Windows

On Windows the same rules are ACLs, which the helper sets and reads back itself rather than trusting an installer to have done it:

  • the socket’s directory, C:\ProgramData\Claimward, gets a protected DACL (nothing inherited from ProgramData, which lets every user create files there): SYSTEM and Administrators in full control, the socket’s group allowed to list and traverse it and nothing more. It is created already carrying that DACL, and a directory that is a junction or a link is refused;
  • the socket gets its own DACL: SYSTEM, Administrators, and the group allowed to connect (read/write);
  • the group is the local group Claimward Users, which the installer creates. If it does not exist the socket is opened to INTERACTIVE (everybody logged on at the machine, console or Remote Desktop) and the helper logs that it did;
  • helper.json must be owned by SYSTEM or Administrators, and writable by nobody else: the helper reads the file’s owner and DACL and refuses any allow entry that grants write, append, delete, WRITE_DAC, WRITE_OWNER or generic write/all to another SID, and a null DACL.

The rules (pkg/helper/acl.go) are pure functions, tested on every platform; the Windows CI job applies them to real files and reads them back.

Approval has a second socket on Windows, C:\ProgramData\Claimward\approve.sock (helper.ListenElevated, served by Server.ServeElevated), whose ACL names SYSTEM and Administrators only: a standard user cannot connect without UAC elevation, and only an approve that arrived there counts. The app reaches it through Client.ElevatedSocketPath and ApproveElevated.

Packaging the polkit policy (Linux)

The Linux package installs packaging/polkit/com.claimward.helper.approve-server.policy of the client repository into /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/. Without it polkit does not know the action and every approval is refused.

Route watches over TLS

A route watch carries the bearer token, so pkg/routeclient runs it over TLS, checked against the system’s roots, except to a loopback address. Against a server whose RouteService is not TLS the handshake fails before the token is sent, and the tunnel stays up without live route updates.

Stopping the helper takes the tunnel down.

item.title: macOS app
item.description:
claimward-vpn-app-osx v0.10.0 is a native app written in Go: one window and a menu-bar status item, drawn by go-widgets, with the system’s own NSTextField and NSPopUpButton for the inputs. There is no webview, no local web server and no JavaScript (before v0.7.0 the window was a Svelte page in a webview). Its logic (sign-in, tenant choice, connect) and its helper are the shared pkg/appcore and pkg/helper; the view model is pkg/appvm, the same one the Linux and Windows apps use.

Design 

 claimward-app (one process, as you)
 ├─ window go-widgets, with NSTextField / NSPopUpButton embedded
 ├─ status item NSStatusItem: status / Open Claimward… / Connect / Disconnect / Quit
 ├─ notifications when the tunnel drops or the session expires (from the app bundle)
 └─ view model pkg/appvm over appcore: sign-in, tenant choice, session
 │ Unix socket (JSON), 0660 root:admin
 ▼
 claimward-helper (root LaunchDaemon)
 enrolls with the server, wireguard-go: utunN, route pushes

The app is one unprivileged process that owns all state. The text input (the server URL) is the system’s text field, with its input method and spell checking; the provider and tenant choices are pop-up buttons. The helper enrolls with the server and owns the tunnel. Closing the window hides it: the app keeps running in the status item and quits through its Quit item.

The window opens at 800 x 480 points (the size of WireGuard’s macOS manager). The Servers sidebar on the left lists the servers, each with its logo (a neutral mark when it has none), its name and its state; +, − and a gear are under the list. Several servers may be connected at once, and each row shows its own state.

The detail panel on the right is a key/value table with section titles, in the manner of WireGuard’s tunnel panel. It hides every empty field except Status and refreshes every second. Server holds the name and logo, the URL, the identity provider and the signed-in identity, the tenant, whether the server is exclusive, and whether the helper has approved it. Status has an icon and the Connect / Disconnect buttons. Interface holds the address and the lease expiry in relative time. Edit is at the bottom right. When the server lists several identity providers, sign-in shows one button per provider.

+ opens a window of its own with only a URL field. Next asks the server for its public discovery document and previews its name, logo, providers and whether it is exclusive; the person confirms before the server is added, and a server that does not answer as a Claimward server is told in plain words. The gear (or Edit) opens the same window on the selected server, prefilled, and can change its identity provider; it is disabled, with the reason in its accessible label, while no server is selected.

Connect on a server the helper has not approved asks macOS for an administrator’s authorization, naming the server’s host, then approves the server and connects (see server approval). A refusal is shown as such. − offers to revoke the approval with the removal. An exclusive server, or a connection that blocks the others, disables Connect and says why, for instance “Alpha is connected and exclusive”.

Build

With go-task:

task config:init # a starter config.json (local Dex)
task install-helper SERVER=https://vpn.example.org # build and install the helper (sudo)
task start:bundle # build Claimward.app and open it

Run the bundle rather than the bare binary: notifications are refused to a process that is not in an app bundle, so from a bare binary a dropped tunnel only reaches the log. By hand (no Node toolchain any more):

CGO_ENABLED=1 go build -o bin/claimward-app ./cmd/claimward-app
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o bin/claimward-helper ./cmd/claimward-helper

Configure

Nothing has to be written by hand: + adds a server by its URL. The app keeps the list in ~/Library/Application Support/Claimward/config.json (app v0.10.0 and later, client v0.11.0; the format is described on the client page):

{
 "version": 2,
 "servers": [
 {"url": "https://vpn.example.com"}
 ]
}

Only the server URL is configured; the providers come from the server. With GitHub and go-authn, clicking Connect shows a code to enter at the displayed page; with OIDC the browser opens the provider’s sign-in page. Older builds (client v0.9.0 and earlier) read server_url, provider, github_client_id, oidc_issuer and oidc_client_id instead; a file in that format is migrated once, on first start, and its session is adopted by the matching server.

Install the helper and run 

sudo ./scripts/install-helper.sh https://vpn.example.org # more servers may follow
open dist/Claimward.app # then click Connect

The installer copies the helper to /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/, writes /Library/Application Support/Claimward/helper.json (root’s, mode 0644) with the servers given, and loads the LaunchDaemon com.claimward.helper. The helper’s socket is /var/run/claimward-helper.sock, 0660, root:admin; it logs to /var/log/claimward-helper.log. sudo ./scripts/uninstall-helper.sh removes it.

Tenants

A person in several tenants chooses one in the detail panel’s Tenant pop-up, which lists them once the server has offered them; Refresh asks again. The choice holds for the session; a new sign-in forgets it. A Connect from the menu bar that the server refuses for want of a choice opens the window.

Release

.github/workflows/release.yml builds Claimward.dmg on v* tags and attaches it to the release. When the signing secrets are set it signs the app with a Developer ID and notarizes and staples the DMG; without them it falls back to an ad-hoc signature, which Gatekeeper blocks on a downloaded DMG. The repository holds no signing secrets, so the published DMGs (v0.1.0 and v0.2.0) are ad-hoc signed and not notarized. The DMG holds the app (with the helper binary inside it); the helper is installed as above.

Still to come: the helper installed with SMJobBless, a release signed with a Developer ID, and DNS applied on macOS.

Session and servers

The session (tokens and the device’s WireGuard key) lives in session.enc, sealed with AES-GCM; the key is held in the login Keychain. It is never written to disk in clear and there is no plaintext fallback: if the Keychain is locked or unavailable (client v0.5.0 and later), sign-in fails with an error saying so. A 0600 session.json from an older version is moved into the store on first start, or deleted if that fails.

The tunnel MTU is the server’s mtu, lowered to fit the path to the server (the interface MTU towards its endpoint, minus 60 for IPv4 or 80 for IPv6) and never below 1280 (client v0.6.0, pkg/pathmtu).

The server must be an https URL. Since v0.7.0 there is no loopback UI API and no launch token: the window and the logic share one process.

item.title: Linux app
item.description:
claimward-vpn-app-linux v0.7.0 is a window and a tray icon drawn in pure Go with go-widgets: no webview, no cgo (CGO_ENABLED=0). The four settings text fields are native GTK 4 entries (system input methods, selection, clipboard), loaded at run time without cgo; the desktop entry starts the app with GO_WIDGETS_GTK=1. Without libgtk-4 the app falls back to painted fields. The native fields show no placeholder text. A privileged helper run by systemd owns the WireGuard tunnel. The logic is the macOS app’s: both use pkg/appcore and pkg/helper.

Design 

 claimward-app (your session)
 ├─ internal/view go-widgets/toolkit widgets, bound with go-widgets/mvvmtk
 ├─ internal/trayview tray icon + menu (StatusNotifierItem over D-Bus)
 ├─ internal/viewmodel all state as go-widgets/mvvm observables and commands
 └─ appcore sign-in, tenant, session; drives the helper
 │ X11 / Wayland │ unix socket, JSON, 0660 root:claimward
 ▼ ▼
 the window, the tray claimward-helper (root, systemd)
 enrolls with a configured server,
 wireguard-go TUN + ip(8), route pushes

The app runs as you and never touches the network configuration or the server itself: everything goes through the helper. The view model holds every piece of state and imports no widget; CI enforces MVVM with mvvmlint and “no hand-drawn UI” with bricolint.

What it does

  • Status: who is signed in, connected or not, the address and interface, the session’s tenant, whether the helper answers, the server. It is polled every 2 seconds. The screens, what each button may do and the poll are the shared pkg/appvm of the client (v0.7.0), which the app’s view model only adapts to observables.
  • Notifications: when the tunnel drops, or the session expires, the app sends a desktop notification, once per change; clicking it opens the window. Your own Disconnect and Sign out are not announced, and a notification that cannot be sent is logged and changes nothing.
  • Sign in: for a device flow the window shows the code and an Open sign-in page button (xdg-open); the sign-in can be cancelled.
  • Tenant: when the server refuses a connection because the person belongs to several, the window says so and offers a drop-down; Choose tenant asks for the list ahead of time. The tenant cannot be changed while connected.
  • Connect / Disconnect / Sign out, Settings (server URL, provider, GitHub client ID, OIDC issuer and client ID), and the connection log.
  • Tray: a status line, Connect, Disconnect, Open window, Quit; the icon is in colour while connected. Closing the window leaves the app in the tray; Quit leaves the tunnel as it is.

The tray needs a StatusNotifierItem host (KDE Plasma, GNOME with the AppIndicator and KStatusNotifierItem Support extension, waybar…). Without one, or if the tray item cannot be put on the session bus, the app says so on start-up and closing the window quits it.

Install

Build as yourself (Go 1.27.4 or later), then install as root:

CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -o bin/ ./cmd/...
sudo ./scripts/install.sh --server https://vpn.example.com

--server accepts https URLs only: the sign-in token is sent to that server, so a plain http:// URL is refused.

install.sh:

  1. creates the claimward group and adds you to it ($SUDO_USER, or --user): log out and back in for it to apply;
  2. installs claimward-app to /usr/local/bin and claimward-helper to /usr/local/sbin (--prefix to change);
  3. writes /etc/claimward/helper.json, root:root, mode 0644, with the server given (an existing file is kept);
  4. installs and starts claimward-helper.service, and waits for its socket;
  5. installs the desktop entry and the icon.

Start Claimward VPN from the desktop’s menu; claimward-app -hidden starts in the tray (for an autostart entry). sudo ./scripts/uninstall.sh removes it all and stops the helper, which takes the tunnel down; --purge also removes /etc/claimward and the group.

Configure

The app: ~/.config/Claimward/config.json, written by the settings form, mode 0600, overridden by CLAIMWARD_* variables (see the client library). The session (tokens and the device’s WireGuard key) is sealed with AES-GCM in session.enc; the key is kept in the desktop’s Secret Service keyring through secret-tool. It is never written to disk in clear. A Secret Service provider is required (client v0.5.0 and later): install and unlock one such as gnome-keyring or KeePassXC, and install secret-tool (libsecret-tools). Without one, sign-in fails with an error naming what is missing; there is no plaintext fallback, on a headless server either. A session.json left by an older version is moved into the keyring on first start, or deleted if the keyring refuses it.

The tunnel MTU is the server’s mtu, lowered to fit the path to the server (the interface MTU towards its endpoint, minus 60 for IPv4 or 80 for IPv6) and never below 1280 (client v0.6.0, pkg/pathmtu).

The helper: /etc/claimward/helper.json (see Privileged helper); after editing it, sudo systemctl restart claimward-helper.

The hardened unit

claimward-helper.service keeps only CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW and CAP_CHOWN, with NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict and only /run writable, ProtectHome, /dev/net/tun alone from /dev, address families limited to unix, inet, inet6 and netlink, and the @system-service system calls. systemd-analyze security claimward-helper rates it 2.5 (OK). Being in the claimward group means being allowed to bring the VPN up and down.

Verified in an Ubuntu 24.04 (arm64) virtual machine against a stand-in server. Not yet verified, according to the README: a real GNOME or KDE desktop, Wayland, HiDPI, a sign-in against a real identity provider, and a real claimward-vpn-server.

item.title: Windows app
item.description:
claimward-vpn-app-windows v0.8.0 is a desktop app with a notification-area (tray) icon. Everything is Go with CGO_ENABLED=0: the window and the tray are drawn by go-widgets (no webview, no HTTP server in the app), except the four settings text fields, which are native Win32 Edit controls (system input method editors, selection, clipboard; they show no placeholder text), and the tunnel is wireguard-go on a Wintun adapter, configured through the IP Helper API. Its logic and helper are the shared pkg/appcore and pkg/helper.

Design 

 claimward-app.exe (the person, unprivileged)
 ├─ internal/ui/view.go widgets, bound by go-widgets/mvvmtk to …
 ├─ internal/ui/viewmodel.go … the ViewModel: all state, observables and commands
 ├─ internal/ui/tray_binding the tray menu, bound to the same ViewModel
 └─ appcore sign-in, session, tenant, helper client
 │ AF_UNIX socket, one JSON request each: C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.sock
 ▼
 claimward-helper.exe — the ClaimwardHelper service (LocalSystem)
 pkg/helper enrolls with a server helper.json names, owns the tunnel
 pkg/wgtun wireguard-go on the Wintun adapter "Claimward"; address, routes, DNS, MTU

The window shows the connection, the address and interface, who is signed in, the tenant and whether the helper answers; the device-flow prompt with a button that opens the page in the default browser (only an https page is ever handed to the shell); Connect / Disconnect / Sign out; Choose tenant; the settings, saved to %AppData%\Claimward\config.json; and the connection log. The status is polled every 2 seconds, by the shared pkg/appvm of the client (v0.7.0), which also decides what each button may do. When the tunnel drops, or the session expires, the app sends a notification once per change; clicking it opens the window (your own Disconnect is not announced). The tray menu offers the status, Connect, Disconnect, Open and Quit. Closing the window quits the app; the tunnel belongs to the service and stays up until Disconnect.

The tray icon appears from v0.3.0. Before it, the tray library had no Windows implementation of the call the app makes, and the app ignored the error, so v0.1.0 and v0.2.0 showed no tray icon. v0.3.0 is built with the tray library that implements it (go-widgets/tray v0.14.0). That is checked by compilation and the library’s own tests, not yet on a Windows desktop. Two known gaps: an icon that cannot be added is reported on stderr, which a windowed build does not show (#6), and quitting may leave a ghost icon until the pointer passes over it (go-widgets/tray#37).

Install

From a release folder (scripts/package.sh builds them, with Wintun), in an elevated PowerShell:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass
.\install.ps1 -Server https://vpn.example.org
# optionally, the app's settings for the current user as well:
.\install.ps1 -Server https://vpn.example.org -Provider github -GitHubClientId Iv1.0123456789abcdef

It copies the programs and wintun.dll to C:\Program Files\Claimward, creates the local group Claimward Users and adds you to it, writes C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.json (after checking that directory, see below), registers and starts the ClaimwardHelper service, and adds a Claimward VPN Start Menu shortcut. Membership takes effect at your next sign-in to Windows; until then the socket refuses you. Add other people with Add-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Claimward Users' -Member <name>.

-Server accepts https URLs only: the sign-in token is sent to that server.

ProgramData lets every user create directories, so the installer refuses a pre-existing C:\ProgramData\Claimward that is a reparse point (a link) or that is not owned by SYSTEM (S-1-5-18) or Administrators (S-1-5-32-544): inspect and remove it, then run the installer again.

.\uninstall.ps1 removes the service, the shortcut and the programs; -RemoveData also removes C:\ProgramData\Claimward and the group. There is no MSI yet.

package.sh downloads wintun-0.14.1.zip from wintun.net and refuses it unless its SHA-256 matches the one pinned in the script; the DLL is signed by WireGuard LLC and is not in the repository.

Configure

The app reads %AppData%\Claimward\config.json, then CLAIMWARD_* variables (see the client library). The session is sealed with DPAPI in a per-user file, session.dpapi, under %AppData%\claimward. It is never written in clear and there is no plaintext fallback: if DPAPI fails (client v0.5.0 and later), sign-in fails with an error saying so. A session.json from an older version is moved into DPAPI on first start, or deleted if that fails.

The tunnel MTU is the server’s mtu, lowered to fit the path to the server (the interface MTU towards its endpoint, minus 60 for IPv4 or 80 for IPv6) and never below 1280 (client v0.6.0, pkg/pathmtu).

The helper reads C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.json:

{
 "servers": ["https://vpn.example.org"],
 "group": "Claimward Users",
 "socket": "C:\\ProgramData\\Claimward\\helper.sock"
}

The service logs to C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.log; from an elevated console, claimward-helper run runs it in the foreground. The ACLs the helper sets and checks are described under Privileged helper.

Still to come: an MSI installer.

item.title: Architecture
item.description:
Claimward separates a control plane, the server, from the data plane, the WireGuard tunnel between a device and the gateway. Authentication is delegated to your identity provider: Claimward never sees a password.

On a device, an unprivileged app signs the person in and keeps the session; a privileged helper (root, or SYSTEM on Windows) enrolls with the server and owns the tunnel. The app never talks to the server itself.

End-to-end enrollment flow 

 ┌──────────┐ 1. sign-in: GitHub device flow, OIDC code + PKCE, ┌──────────┐
 │ app │ or go-authn device flow (+ key registration) │ IdP │
 │ (as you) │◀─────────────────── bearer token ──────────────────│ │
 └────┬─────┘ └──────────┘
 │ 2. socket: connect {server_url, bearer, private key, tenant}
 ▼
 ┌──────────┐ 3. POST /api/v1/enroll ┌─────────────────────────┐
 │ helper │ Authorization: Bearer <token> │ claimward-vpn-server │
 │ (root) │ {public_key, device, tenant} ───▶ │ verify the bearer │
 │ │ │ choose the tenant │
 │ │ ◀─── 4. {assigned_ip, │ allocate an address │
 │ │ server_public_key, endpoint, │ wgctrl: add the peer │
 │ │ allowed_ips, dns, │ (AllowedIPs = ip/32) │
 │ │ grpc_endpoint, keepalive, └───────────┬─────────────┘
 │ │ lease_expires_at} │ RouteService
 │ │ ◀═════════════ 6. gRPC Watch (TLS) ═══════════════╛ (live routes)
 │ │
 │ │ 5. wireguard-go: utunN / Wintun "Claimward", address, routes
 └────┬─────┘
 ╚═══════════════════ WireGuard tunnel ════════════════════▶ private network
  1. The app signs the person in with the configured provider: GitHub by default (OAuth device flow), any OpenID Connect issuer (authorization code with PKCE, in the browser), or a go-authn provider (device flow). The bearer it gets is a GitHub access token, an OIDC ID token, or a go-authn access token. With go-authn, the device’s public key is first registered at the provider, and the bearer is the token that registration returns.
  2. The app generates the device’s WireGuard key pair at the first sign-in and keeps it in its encrypted session file (session.enc, whose key is in the Keychain or the Secret Service; session.dpapi on Windows) until the person signs out, so the device keeps its public key across connections (and its address while it is enrolled). To connect, it hands the helper the server URL, the bearer, the private key and the tenant chosen for the session, over the helper’s socket.
  3. The helper checks that the server is one its own configuration names, then calls POST /api/v1/enroll with the device’s public key and the bearer.
  4. The server verifies the bearer (a GitHub API call, an OIDC ID token, or a go-authn access token whose subject must own the key), applies any organisation or email-domain allowlist, picks the tenant, allocates a VPN address and programs the gateway (wgctrl) with a peer whose only allowed IP is that /32. It answers with the tunnel parameters: the address, its own public key, the endpoint, the tenant’s routes and DNS servers, the keepalive, the RouteService endpoint and the lease’s end.
  5. The helper brings up a userspace tunnel with wireguard-go, gives the interface its address and installs the routes.
  6. When the server advertises a RouteService (GRPC_ENDPOINT), the helper watches it over gRPC: route changes made to the tenant reach the device without enrolling again.

Leases

Each enrollment carries a lease of LEASE_TTL (24 hours by default). A background reaper on the server removes, every minute, the peers whose lease has ended, so a lost or revoked device falls off the gateway on its own. With go-authn a lease never outlives the key’s registration at the provider.

The server renews a lease on POST /api/v1/heartbeat, and removes a peer at once on POST /api/v1/deregister.

From claimward-vpn-client v0.3.1, that is from the app releases that carry it (the macOS, Linux and Windows apps from v0.2.0), the helper keeps the lease itself while the tunnel is up. It renews at half of what the lease has left, never sooner than 30 seconds nor later than 10 minutes, and acts on the answer:

The server answers The helper
a renewed lease renews again at half of it
404 not_enrolled: it forgot the device (the lease ran out, or the server restarted) enrolls again with the same key and tenant, and brings the tunnel up from that answer; if that fails too, takes the tunnel down
403 (not_a_member, key_not_registered): access withdrawn takes the tunnel down, and reports why (last_error)
401, a 5xx, or nothing retries within a minute, sooner than the lease ends

The helper renews with the last bearer it was given. That is enough for a GitHub token, not for a go-authn access token, which expires in minutes and which only the app can refresh. So while the app runs, pkg/appcore hands the helper a fresh bearer (the helper’s renew action) at 40% of what the lease has left (at most 8 minutes apart), before the helper’s own renewal is due. An app restarted under a running tunnel starts doing so at its first status poll.

Disconnect (the helper’s down) deregisters the peer, giving its address back at once. A helper that is stopping (its service manager stops it, or the machine shuts down) takes the tunnel down without deregistering, so a helper restarted finds the lease still there, and a stopped machine’s lease runs out on the server.

The v0.1.0 apps are built on earlier client versions, which do none of this: they renew a lease only by connecting again, and leave the peer on the gateway after Disconnect until its lease ends.

Trust boundaries

  • The server is the only component that talks to the identity provider to verify a sign-in, and the only one with rights to change the gateway’s peers.
  • On the device, the helper is the only privileged process. Anything that can reach its socket can ask it to act, so it acts within its own configuration: it enrolls only with the servers that configuration names and takes no tunnel configuration from a request. See Privileged helper.
  • The app runs as the person. It holds the session (bearer token and device key) in an encrypted file, never in clear on disk: sealed with a key kept in the macOS Keychain or the Linux Secret Service, or with Windows DPAPI. With no usable store, sign-in fails.
  • A route watch carries the bearer token, so it runs over TLS except to a loopback address.
  • The wire contract lives in one place, claimward-vpn-client/pkg/protocol and pkg/routespb, imported by both the clients and the server.

item.title: Server approval
item.description:
The helper runs as root (SYSTEM on Windows) and a server it enrolls with chooses the routes and the peer of the machine’s tunnel: a hostile server is every packet of the machine, sent there. Since client v0.11.0 the helper takes a server from the app only if one of these holds:

  1. the administrator’s configuration names it (servers in helper.json, now optional: the pre-approval);
  2. it was approved before, and still says what it said then;
  3. it is approved now, with the consent of the operating system, obtained by the helper itself.

An app flag, a field of the request, or a claim of any kind is never consent.

What is asked of the system

Platform Consent
macOS Authorization Services right com.claimward.helper.approve-server, rule authenticate-admin-nonshared: an administrator’s name and password, every time. The app obtains the authorization (macauth.Obtain) and sends its 32-byte external form; the helper has the system verify it and destroys it, so one token buys one approval. A forged token names nothing in the system and is refused
Linux polkit action com.claimward.helper.approve-server (auth_admin), asked of the system bus for the process behind the socket: its pid from SO_PEERCRED and its start time from /proc/<pid>/stat, which defeats pid reuse. The policy file ships in packaging/polkit/ and goes in /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/
Windows a second socket, C:\ProgramData\Claimward\approve.sock, whose ACL names SYSTEM and Administrators only: a standard user cannot connect without UAC elevation. Only a request that came in on it counts

With no authorizer configured the helper refuses every approval: it fails closed. A request that is refused, or that the system cannot answer, changes nothing.

What is remembered

The helper keeps the approved servers in a file only root can write:

Platform File
macOS /var/db/claimward/approved-servers.json
Linux /var/lib/claimward/approved-servers.json
Windows C:\ProgramData\Claimward\approved-servers.json

Each entry is the server’s canonical URL and the SHA-256 of its discovery identity: its name and its identity providers (id, kind, issuer, client ids). A server that changes one of those is not the one that was approved: the helper refuses it (server_identity_changed) until it is approved again. Whether the server is exclusive, its logo and the providers’ display names are not part of the identity, and neither is its TLS certificate, which is renewed every few weeks (the connection is verified against the web PKI at each use).

The file is read afresh at every use, so deleting it, or removing a line, revokes at once; the revoke action does the same for one server. An administrator’s servers list is never edited by the helper.

Errors the app sees

Code Meaning
server_not_approved the server is neither pre-approved nor approved: ask the person to approve it
server_identity_changed it was approved, and no longer says the same: approve it again
approval_denied the system’s consent was not given

Limits, stated

  • On macOS the text of the prompt is supplied by the app that asks, so a hostile process in the socket’s group can make the system ask an administrator to approve its own server, and a distracted administrator can say yes. The credential is an administrator’s, never cached, and good for one approval.
  • On Windows, an elevated process can approve anything, as an administrator can edit the file anyway.
  • Linux has no cache either: auth_admin asks every time.
